content: Pelvic lymphadenectomy is a surgical procedure that provides prognostic information for patients diagnosed with endometrial cancer. This information can influence decisions regarding adjuvant treatment. However, studies have not demonstrated a therapeutic benefit of lymphadenectomy, and the procedure is associated with significant morbidity. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is a technique that identifies the first lymph node draining from a cancer site, which is then examined histologically for cancer cell involvement. This method is widely used in other cancers, such as breast and vulvar cancers. Various tracers are employed for SLNB, including radioactive technetium-99m, blue dyes like patent blue or methylene blue, and near-infrared fluorescent dyes such as indocyanine green (ICG). These tracers can be used individually or in combination to detect sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs). The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of SLNB in identifying pelvic lymph node involvement in women with presumed early-stage endometrial cancer prior to surgery. The study also aimed to assess the detection rate of SLNs. A comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE and Embase, was conducted, covering studies published up to July 2019. Studies were included if they assessed the diagnostic accuracy of SLNB tracers against a reference standard of histological examination of pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes following systematic lymphadenectomy. Two independent reviewers screened studies for inclusion, assessed their methodological quality using the QUADAS-2 tool, and extracted data. The detection rate was calculated as the mean proportion of SLNs identified out of the total number of women included in the studies. Sensitivity estimates were pooled using meta-analytical methods, and the results were summarized using the GRADE approach. The search identified 6,259 unique records, of which 232 studies were reviewed in full text. Ultimately, 33 studies involving 2,237 women were included in the analysis. These studies used various tracers: 11 studies used blue dye alone, 4 used technetium-99m alone, 12 used a combination of blue dye and technetium-99m, 9 used ICG with near-infrared fluorescence, and 1 used a combination of ICG and technetium-99m. The overall quality of reporting in most studies was poor, leading to a high proportion of unclear risk of bias ratings. The mean SLN detection rate across all studies was 86.9% (95% CI 82.9% to 90.8%), based on moderate-certainty evidence. For studies reporting bilateral detection, the mean rate was 65.4% (95% CI 57.8% to 73.0%). Detection rates varied depending on the tracer used, ranging from 77.8% (95% CI 70.0% to 85.6%) for blue dye alone to 100% for the combination of ICG and technetium-99m, although the latter was based on a single study with very low-certainty evidence. The rate of positive lymph nodes identified ranged from 5.2% to 34.4%, with a mean of 20.1% (95% CI 17.7% to 22.3%). The pooled sensitivity of SLNB was 91.8% (95% CI 86.5% to 95.1%), based on moderate-certainty evidence. Sensitivity estimates for individual tracers were as follows: blue dye alone, 95.2% (95% CI 77.2% to 99.2%); technetium-99m alone, 90.5% (95% CI 67.7% to 97.7%); blue dye and technetium-99m combined, 91.9% (95% CI 74.4% to 97.8%); ICG alone, 92.5% (95% CI 81.8% to 97.1%); ICG and blue dye combined, 90.5% (95% CI 63.2% to 98.1%); and ICG with technetium-99m, 100% (95% CI 63% to 100%). Meta-regression analyses revealed no significant differences in sensitivity between the different tracers, between studies with predominantly FIGO stage 1A versus 1B or higher, between studies assessing only the pelvic lymph node basin versus both pelvic and para-aortic basins, or between studies using subserosal injection alone versus subserosal and cervical injection. Importantly, false-positive results cannot occur in this context, as histological examination of the SLN is not influenced by findings from additional nodes removed during systematic lymphadenectomy. In conclusion, SLNB using ICG alone or in combination with technetium-99m or blue dye demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity for detecting lymph node involvement in endometrial cancer. Detection rates appear to be higher with ICG or combinations of ICG and technetium-99m. However, the role of SLNB in guiding treatment decisions, particularly in comparison to approaches based on uterine factors and molecular profiling, requires further investigation in high-quality interventional studies.
